title: India's 'Cockroach' Protesters Force Government Talks as NEET Paper Leak Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Youth-led movement begins negotiations with Modi government as Delhi shuts metro stations and internet, marking the biggest challenge to the prime minister since 2014.
body:
• Leaders of India's self-named Cockroach Janta Party began formal talks with the government on Friday after weeks of street protests demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the NEET paper leak.
  • Delhi authorities shut 17 metro stations and cut mobile internet services for a third time this week as tens of thousands of protesters camped in the capital.
  • PM Modi said the cabinet would discuss draft legislation to toughen penalties for exam paper leaks, but protesters rejected the proposal as insufficient.
  • The NEET entrance exam taken by 2 million students on May 3 was cancelled after its question paper leaked; a re-exam was held on June 21.

Leaders of India's youth-led "cockroach" movement sat down with senior government ministers on Friday in an attempt to resolve a crisis that has paralysed the capital and forced the suspension of parliamentary proceedings — but vowed to keep protesting until Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.

Two leaders of the self-named Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) met with two government ministers at the Constitution Club near parliament, hours after activist Sonam Wangchuk ended a 26-day hunger strike overnight, according to Reuters. It was the second round of talks since Monday.

"This is now a mass movement. The CJP will continue its protest until Pradhan resigns. This is the only solution to bring this to an end."

— Abhijeet Dipke, CJP founder

From Online Satire to National Uprising

The movement began as an online satire involving a few hundred young people but has mushroomed into the biggest youth challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi since he took office in 2014. The immediate trigger was the cancellation of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), India's undergraduate medical entrance exam, after question papers from the May 3 test were found to have leaked. About 2 million students were affected, with about a dozen suicides linked to the cancellation, according to Reuters.

https://x.com/CNNnews18/status/2080597952054321627

A re-exam was held on June 21, with results declared on July 16, but those results have also come under scrutiny. A student in Beed, Maharashtra moved the Bombay High Court alleging a mismatch between his expected and actual re-test scores — his self-calculated 508 marks versus the NTA-issued scorecard showing 95. In Madhya Pradesh, another candidate challenged the NTA's constitutional validity after discovering a 241-mark discrepancy between two different OMR response sheets on the official portal, according to LiveLaw.

Protests Shut Down the Capital

Tens of thousands of young protesters marched on parliament on Monday in violation of a ban, clashing with police who deployed tear gas and batons. Violence was reported again on Wednesday night when over 10,000 protesters gathered at the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi.

Authorities responded by shutting 17 Delhi Metro stations on Friday morning — the third large-scale closure this week of a system that serves as the capital's lifeline. Mobile internet services in central Delhi were disrupted again, with the government extending the shutdown until midnight Friday, two industry sources told Reuters.

Protests spread beyond Delhi to Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata, Goa, Guwahati, Thiruvananthapuram, Jammu, and Ahmedabad. Resident doctors' associations from Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Telangana, and West Bengal issued statements demanding accountability for the paper leak under the banner of the Federation of All India Medical Association, according to Careers360.

Government Under Pressure on Multiple Fronts

Opposition lawmakers led by Rahul Gandhi staged a protest at parliament on Wednesday, many dressed in black and carrying placards reading "Our children's future is not for sale" and "Save lives, Stop NEET." The protest forced a temporary suspension of proceedings. On Tuesday, police detained Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, and several senior Congress leaders during a sit-in outside the prime minister's residence, releasing them late that evening.

Pradhan, breaking his silence on demands for his resignation, said on X that the government was "100% committed to discussing NEET and addressing every genuine concern of our youth on the floor of the House." Modi said the federal cabinet would meet Friday to discuss a draft amending laws to punish those responsible for paper leaks.

But protesters rejected the proposal. "The examination system should be fixed to prevent leaks in the first place," the movement's leaders said, according to Reuters.

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

NEET is the sole gateway to roughly 150,000 undergraduate medical seats across India, making it one of the country's highest-stakes examinations. Families in the Indian diaspora with children considering medical education in India are directly affected by the turmoil. The crisis has deepened questions about the credibility of the National Testing Agency, which also administers entrance exams for engineering and other professional courses that diaspora families rely on for pathways back into India's educational system.

Analysts warn the government must go beyond words to address the crisis. "Student-led protests risk spiralling into a larger political and social challenge for the Modi government, as it has touched a raw nerve among a young, growing workforce that is struggling to find jobs," said Shumita Deveshwar, chief India economist at consultancy TS Lombard. With key state elections in Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Punjab next year, the political stakes are high.
